Haft
HAFT
noun
From the Saxon haeft, a handle, from habban, to have or hold — that part of a tool or weapon which the hand takes. The same root gives the German Heft and stands behind our have.

Biblical Definition

The haft is the handle of a blade, and it occurs once, in a scene of deliberate and gruesome detail. Ehud, the left-handed judge, has made himself a two-edged dagger of a cubit length and hidden it on his right thigh where no guard would search; he draws it with the wrong hand and drives it into Eglon king of Moab: “And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly” (Jdg 3:22). The whole weapon disappeared — not merely the edge but the handle, so that Ehud left it inside and went out, locking the doors behind him. The narrator is not being sensational for its own sake. The book of Judges records Israel’s deliverances in their actual grimness, and this one is granted through a man with a disability turned to advantage, a concealed weapon, and eighteen years of tribute-paying patience. Scripture does not romanticise its deliverers, and the reader who wants his heroes clean will find Judges intolerable. That is a mercy, not a defect. A book that told only of blameless saints would have nothing to say to the actual church, and the God of Judges is repeatedly shown raising up flawed and unlikely men because Israel cried unto Him, not because they deserved better.

Webster 1828 Definition

The handle of a knife, dagger, or tool — the part taken by the hand, as distinguished from the blade.

HAFT, n. A handle; that part of an instrument which is taken into the hand.

From the Saxon haeft, a handle, from habban, to have, to hold.

Distinguished from the blade, edge, or head of the instrument.

HAFT, v.t. To set in a haft; to furnish with a handle.

Jdg 3:22: the haft went in after the blade, so that the dagger could not be drawn out.

Key Scripture

Jdg 3:21 — "And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly:"

Jdg 3:22 — "And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly; and the dirt came out."

Jdg 2:16 — "Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them."

Jdg 3:15 — "But when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded : and by him the children of Israel sent a present unto Eglon the king of Moab."

Modern Corruption

The narrative books are sanitised for teaching — their violence trimmed and their deliverers tidied — which quietly substitutes a gallery of moral examples for the God who raises up flawed men.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding distortion is the moral-example method of reading Scripture. Judges is retold for children with the daggers removed, and preached to adults as a series of leadership lessons, so that the question put to the text becomes what should I imitate here? Ask that of Ehud and you get nothing usable. Ask it of Samson, Jephthah, or Gideon and you get less. The book resists the method on purpose. Its refrain is that Israel did evil, was sold into the hand of an oppressor, cried unto the LORD, and the LORD raised up a deliverer — four movements in which the only constant actor is God.

Recover the plain sense: the point of the haft disappearing into Eglon is that the deliverance was real, physical, and unlovely, and that God gave it to a people who had earned eighteen years of servitude. Heb 11 later names Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among the faithful without pretending they were admirable in everything, which is exactly how Scripture handles its saints — Noah drunk, Abraham lying, David worse. To sand these accounts down is to lose the doctrine they were written to teach: that salvation comes from outside the sinner, and that God’s choice of instruments is governed by His mercy rather than by their merit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon haeft, a handle — the part the hand holds; buried with the blade in Eglon’s belly.

expand to see more

Haft — Saxon haeft, a handle, from habban, to hold.

Kin to the German Heft and to English have.

The handle as distinguished from the blade or head.

Jdg 3:22: haft and blade both entered; the weapon was left inside.

Ehud was left-handed and wore the dagger on the right thigh — concealment by exception.

Usage

"Judges records its deliverances in their real grimness, without tidying the deliverers."

"The refrain of the book puts the constancy on God’s side, not the judge’s."

"Heb 11 names these men as faithful without pretending they were exemplary throughout."
